prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated at once and bring optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B019 to B042. In round 1 I said B042 was my fallback if B019 was judged premature, and the exchange has moved me, for scientific reasons and not because five colleagues prefer it. The decisive point is the one the chair put to Kroll: the lattice clock is separable from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes because the magic-wavelength condition lets a large ensemble be interrogated without Doppler, recoil or light-shift penalties. As a statistical physicist I find that the real step. Averaging over N independent atoms lowers the quantum projection noise, and with an ultrastable laser this is what turns the clock from a single-ion accuracy device into a stability device that can resolve fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 in hours instead of weeks. That is an original conceptual idea (Katori) followed by a decisive realisation of its performance (Ye), reproduced in several independent laboratories and compared across fibre links. Ye's use of combs and cavity-stabilised lasers is an enabling tool, as it was for everyone in the field, and does not by itself make the clock a mere application of 2005. The two-name credit is clean and leaves room within the three-person limit. I still regard B019 as the case with the larger conceptual reach, but I cannot say the discovery criterion is met with the same confidence when the pairing mechanism and the sample dependence are still open.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining reservation about B042 is the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes. A citation that says only 'precision clocks' would invite the objection that we are honouring the same toolbox twice, so the wording must be anchored on the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation, not on optical frequency metrology in general. The second is credit: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others made real contributions, and none of us has checked the priority record for the first proposal and first demonstration in detail. I cannot do so from my own field and rely on colleagues in atomic physics. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, though I regard that as a policy step independent of the science. Against my own earlier choice, B019 is eight years old, the pairing mechanism is unsettled, and results depend on twist-angle disorder and sample quality, so a few more years of consolidation would be reasonable, even if it is not costless.

responses.point: Kroll put B042 first and the chair asked him whether the stability gained by interrogating many atoms at once is the decisive point of separation from the 2005 comb prize. He also asked that the citation be written around the lattice-clock concept and its realisation at 1e-18 and that members outside atomic physics test the case.
responses.response: Testing it from outside atomic physics, I agree that the many-atom interrogation is the decisive separation. Statistical averaging over a large ensemble, made possible by the magic-wavelength trap, is what gives stability that single-ion clocks cannot match, and it is not a property of combs or of ion control. That is why I now accept your wording, built on the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation. I would still say that Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work is an enabling technology and the citation should not mention it, so that no overlap with 2005 is claimed. Your own caveat that you have not checked current best uncertainties is fair, and I cannot check them either; I rely on the candidate summaries.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers DMFT (B033), lists B042 and B019 as alternatives, and argues that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened so recognition could wait. He also doubted B019 because of the pairing mechanism, disorder and the omitted experimental first authors.
responses.response: On the waiting argument for B042 I disagree. The science is confirmed regardless of whether the redefinition is adopted, and a prize for a discovery should not depend on a metrological convention decided elsewhere. On B019 you are right and I concede part of the point: the pairing mechanism and sample dependence make it less settled than I argued, and that is part of why I have moved. I do not move to B033. I still see DMFT mainly as a framework whose credit chain runs through Metzner outside the trio, and you accept yourself that this is a method and approximation scheme, so it does not fit the discovery wording as cleanly as a measured effect.

responses.point: Olsson found the B019 attribution persuasive but argued from experience with oxide interfaces that a result depending on sample-to-sample structure deserves patience, and that waiting a few years costs little.
responses.response: Your experience with oxide interfaces is the most useful argument I heard against my own position, and it has weight with me because it comes from someone who has seen strongly sample-dependent phenomena settle. I still do not think waiting is costless, since the attribution is currently clean and could change as more groups claim credit, but I accept that the open question about the mechanism is real in a way that has no counterpart in the lattice clock. That, together with your point about the discovery criterion, is why I now put B019 as an alternative. Your own recusal from B028 and your disclosed Japanese links seem appropriately handled, and I see no reason for restraint on B042.

responses.point: Lindroth put B042 first and said the citation should be explicit about the boundary to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; she also noted that Mehlig's second choice is her first, making B042 the safer option while B019 waits for the physics to settle.
responses.response: I accept the observation, though I would not put it as 'safer'. My reason is that the discovery in B042 is already characterised on its own figure of merit and independently reproduced, which I cannot say with the same confidence for B019. Your request that the boundary be explicit in the citation is one I support: the wording should name the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom clock, and not time and frequency measurement in general. I also share your concern about the other strontium and ytterbium groups, and I think the committee has to accept openly that a two-name credit cannot cover them.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, supports B042 and says the committee must state what is genuinely new in the lattice clock, that the citation has to be written narrowly, and that other pioneers such as Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and Takamoto are outside the two names while he relies on memory for the priority history.
responses.response: I agree and it is the question that most needs a documentary answer before a final vote. I raised in round 1 that Ye's record accuracy leans on comb technology, and I would now put it more precisely: the novelty is the neutral-atom magic-wavelength scheme and its demonstration at the highest accuracy, and the comb and laser stabilisation are tools. Whether the early priority between Katori and the other groups can be settled from the published record is something none of us has verified, and I would not present the two-name credit as a finding about priority. I would also support recording in the citation that it recognises the scheme and its realisation, not an exhaustive list of contributors.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B038 for the Cirac-Zoller proposal and Blatt's realisation but concedes B042 is the cleaner case on attribution and that B038 overlaps the 2012 prize, with Wineland and Monroe outside the credited names.
responses.response: I take the Cirac-Zoller idea seriously, and I agree with your own assessment that the attribution is less clean than for B042. The difficulty you state, that Wineland and Monroe have claims the three names sidestep and that the label bundles quantum computing with cold-atom simulation, is one I cannot resolve from outside the field. I would add that B050 already covers the cold-atom side, so a B038 prize would need a narrow scope that no one has yet proposed. On B049 I agree with your decision to hold it as an alternative only because of the 2025 prize and the four-into-three allocation.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record on the first lattice-clock proposal and demonstration supports Katori and Ye as the two credited names, given the possible claims of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others; I cannot check this myself.
Whether the committee will accept that many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength is a distinct invention and not an application of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control toolbox.

Whether B019 will look like the better choice in a few years if the pairing mechanism and sample dependence settle, and whether the junior experimentalists and earlier moire theorists will then be thought to have been wrongly omitted.
Whether the committee will adopt a convention for crediting large collaborations, which would change my view of B057.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. None of the credited candidates for B042, B019 or B057 appears among my documented supervisors, institutions or co-authors. My expertise is statistical physics and complex systems, not atomic physics or moire materials, so on the details of clock metrology and the condensed-matter literature I rely on colleagues. Other members have disclosed connections (Olsson on B028 and Japan, Johansson on B049 and B038, Kroll on Hall and WACQT, Lindroth on the Lund attosecond group); I see nothing among them that requires restraint on B042.
